meta.title: Indus Valley Civilisation Atlas
meta.subtitle: Comprehensive Atlas of Harappan Metropolises, Material Discoveries & Global Bronze Age Trade
meta.period_span: c. 3300 BCE – 1300 BCE (Mature Urban Phase: 2600–1900 BCE)
meta.geographic_extent: Spanning over 1.5 million sq. km across India, Pakistan, Afghanistan, and maritime trading ports in Mesopotamia and the Persian Gulf.
citations: Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) reports and excavation monographs.
Kenoyer, J.M. (1998). Ancient Cities of the Indus Valley Civilization.
Possehl, G.L. (2002). The Indus Civilization: A Contemporary Perspective.
Ratnagar, S. (2001). Understanding Harappa: Civilization in the Greater Indus Valley.
Parpola, A. (1994). Deciphering the Indus Script.
Mahadevan, I. (1977). The Indus Script: Texts, Concordance and Tables.
Rao, S.R. (1973; 1985). Lothal and the Indus Civilization; The Decipherment of the Indus Script.
Bisht, R.S. (2015). Excavations at Dholavira (1989-2005), Archaeological Survey of India.

trade_routes.name: Southern Maritime Route to Dilmun & Mesopotamia
trade_routes.description: The primary ocean-going merchant trade route connecting Lothal and Gujarat ports with Magan (Oman), Dilmun (Bahrain/Failaka), and the Sumerian city of Ur at the head of the Persian Gulf.

trade_routes.name: Northern Inland & Lapis Lazuli Route
trade_routes.description: Overland caravan route passing through Punjab and the Khyber and Hindu Kush passes to the Harappan lapis lazuli outpost of Shortugai on the Amu Darya (Oxus) River.

trade_routes.name: Ghaggar-Hakra River Axis
trade_routes.description: The dense inland urban spine tracing the ancient Ghaggar-Hakra / Saraswati river basin, holding over 60% of all known Harappan settlements.

sites.name: Mohenjo-daro (Mound of the Dead)
sites.badge: UNESCO World Heritage · Largest Urban Center
key_structures: The Great Bath (Mahasnanagar) with bitumen waterproofing
Great Granary / Warehouse with air ducts
College of Priests / Assembly Hall (pillared hall with 20 brick pillars)
Citadel Mound and Lower Town on grid plan
Underground corbelled brick sewer and drainage network
key_artifacts: Bronze 'Dancing Girl' (lost-wax casting)
Steatite bust of the 'Priest-King' with trefoil patterned shawl
Pashupati Seal (M-304) depicting seated horned deity surrounded by animals
Terracotta Mother Goddess figurines
Seven-sign unicorn seals with standard cubical chert weights
sites.foreign_connection: Trade hub connecting Sindh with the Persian Gulf; seals from Mohenjo-daro carry symbols replicated on Gulf seals in Failaka and Ras al-Jinz.
sites.description: The crowning urban jewel of the Indus civilization, housing an estimated 40,000 residents with advanced sanitation, multistory brick courtyards, and zero monumental royal palaces—suggesting a civic republic or merchant governance.

sites.name: Harappa
sites.discovered_by: Dayaram Sahni (1921); M.S. Vats; Sir Mortimer Wheeler
key_structures: Great Granary (two rows of six granaries with ventilation passages)
Circular brick threshing floors for grain processing
Workmen's quarters (barracks for artisans)
Fortified Citadel (Mound AB) with perimeter defense ramparts
Cemetery R-37 and Cemetery H
key_artifacts: Red sandstone torso of a youth / dancer with socketed arms
Grey chert dancing Nataraja-like torso
Vanity case / cosmetic set with copper tweezers and mirrors
Over 1,200 inscribed steatite seals and sealing impressions
Graffiti on potsherds featuring early proto-Indus script
sites.foreign_connection: Northern manufacturing and processing capital along the Ravi-Indus river corridor, funneling timber, wheat, and copper into international caravan routes.
sites.description: The first discovered site giving the civilization its name. Excavations revealed extensive grain storage, craft quarters, and stratified cultural layers spanning from pre-urban Kot Diji phase into mature urbanism.

sites.name: Dholavira (Kotada Timba)
key_structures: Gigantic cascading stone water reservoirs (16 reservoirs holding 250,000 cu.m)
Tripartite city division: Citadel (Castle + Bailey), Middle Town, and Lower Town
Massive stone architecture using dressed limestone blocks (unique in IVC)
Monumental ceremonial ground / stadium (283m long)
Northern gateway chamber where the Dholavira Signboard fell
key_artifacts: The Famous 10-Character Dholavira Signboard (3m long wooden board with giant gypsum letters)
Polished stone pillars and architectural members
Gold beads, ear ornaments, and copper mirrors
Unicorn and composite beast steatite seals
Spoked terracotta wheel and gaming boards
sites.foreign_connection: Key island gateway guarding the Rann of Kutch maritime entry; exported marine shell, chalcedony, and banded agate to Mesopotamia and Magan.
sites.description: An architectural and hydraulic marvel built on an island in the Great Rann of Kutch. Features the earliest known monumental inscription (the Dholavira Signboard) and the ancient world's most sophisticated rainwater harvesting system.

sites.name: Rakhigarhi
sites.period: Early, Mature to Late Harappan (5500–1800 BCE)
key_structures: Eleven archaeological mounds (Mounds 1-11) forming an immense metropolis
Mud-brick fortification walls with bastions
Podium platforms with sacrificial/fire pits and altars
Elaborate lapidary workshop with carnelian and steatite beads
Planned streets with covered public and private drain conduits
key_artifacts: Gold foil jewellery, banded agate, and carnelian bead necklaces
Ancient DNA extracted from 4,500-year-old skeleton (Narasimhan et al. Cell 2019)
Copper fishing hooks, arrowheads, and bronze mirrors
Terracotta wheels, figurines of bulls, and animal seal impressions
Standardized chert balance weights
sites.foreign_connection: Ghaggar-Hakra basin metropolis serving as the premier inland trade hub connecting raw material sources in Rajasthan and the Himalayas with urban consumers across the Saraswati valley.
sites.description: Surpassing Mohenjo-daro in total footprint (spanning over 350 hectares across 11 mounds), Rakhigarhi is the largest known settlement of the Indus Valley Civilisation and a vital source of biomolecular and genetic research.

sites.name: Lothal (Mound of the Dead)
key_structures: Massive burnt-brick tidal dockyard basin (214m x 36m) with lock-gate and spillway
High warehouse complex on a 3.5m elevated mud-brick platform (64 cubical blocks)
Acropolis and Lower Town with bead factory and metal workshops
Drainage system discharging into the dock basin
Cemetery with double burials (joint male-female graves)
key_artifacts: Persian Gulf circular steatite seal (proving direct maritime link to Dilmun)
Terracotta models of masted ocean-going sailing ships
Shell ivory scale (measure of length divided into precise decimal units: 1.704mm)
Lothal bead factory with micro-drills and thousands of carnelian beads
Ivory dice, game boards, and terracotta dogs and horses
sites.foreign_connection: The primary seaport linking the Indus civilization to Mesopotamia (Ur, Kish), Dilmun (Bahrain), and Magan (Oman); exported carnelian, cotton textiles, ivory, and timber in exchange for tin, copper, and silver.
sites.description: The world's oldest engineered tidal dockyard, built along the Gulf of Khambhat. Lothal was the premier maritime export hub for Harappan beadmakers and jewelers trading directly with the Bronze Age Near East.

sites.name: Kalibangan (Black Bangles)
sites.discovered_by: Luigi Pio Tessitori (1914); B.B. Lal and B.K. Thapar (1960-69)
key_structures: The world's earliest furrowed agricultural field (criss-cross plough marks)
Series of seven clay-lined 'fire altars' (havan kundas) on mud-brick platforms
Citadel (fortified rhomboid) and separate Lower Town
Brick-lined circular and rectangular sacrificial pits
Paved streets laid in classic grid pattern with mud-brick walls
key_artifacts: Terracotta black terracotta bangles from which the site gets its name
Cylindrical Mesopotamian-style seal with human and animal figures
Terracotta bull figurine and plough models
Camel bones (earliest record of domestic camel in South Asia)
Inscribed terracotta cakes and pottery showing early Harappan graffiti
sites.foreign_connection: Key trading depot along the Saraswati (Ghaggar) river trade highway; produced grain surpluses and exported black terracotta and shell bangles.
sites.description: Famous for unearthing the earliest recorded ploughed agricultural field in human history (demonstrating two-crop mixed cultivation) and distinctive ritual fire altars.

sites.name: Banawali
key_structures: Radial / star-shaped street layout deviating from strict grid planning
Deep defensive moat encircling the town
High fortified citadel separated from lower township by a rampart
Large multi-room houses equipped with private courtyards and washrooms
key_artifacts: Intact, functional terracotta model of a plough (hal)
Abundant high-yield six-row barley grains (highest concentration in IVC)
Touchstone with gold streaks (used by ancient goldsmiths to test purity)
Inscribed steatite seals and lapis lazuli beads
Clay bangles, shell beads, and copper arrowheads
sites.foreign_connection: Supplied northern agricultural grains (barley, pulses) and processed copper tools into the regional network.
sites.description: Crucial site on the dried bed of the Saraswati river that yielded the world's most complete Harappan terracotta plough model and evidence of sophisticated metallurgy and goldsmithing.

sites.name: Surkotada
key_structures: Stone and rubble fortification wall with rampart and entrance gateway
Interconnected Citadel and Residential Annexure
Pot-burial system with stone slabs covering megalithic-style cairns
key_artifacts: Horse (Equus caballus) bone remains and teeth identified by paleontologist Sandor Bokonyi
Copper chisel, spearhead, and socketed celt
Inscribed seal with unicorn motif
Semi-precious stone beads of agate and carnelian
sites.foreign_connection: Fortified checkpoint guarding caravan access between Sindh and Kutch.
sites.description: A fortified garrison outpost in Kutch renowned among historians for yielding equine skeletal remains in mature Harappan layers.

sites.name: Chanhudaro
key_structures: Industrial workshops exclusively devoted to craft manufacture
Kilns and furnace installations for baking steatite and glazed faience
No fortified citadel (the only major IVC city without a citadel)
key_artifacts: Steatite and carnelian bead-making workshop with specialized micro-drills
Terracotta lipstick and eye paint (kajal / kohl) cosmetic containers
Brick bearing the imprint of a dog's paw chasing a cat
Bronze carts with seated drivers and ornate mirrors
Seal-cutter tools and uncarved seal blanks
sites.foreign_connection: Specialized industrial factory town producing luxury carnelian and micro-steatite beads specifically destined for the royal elites of Sumer and Akkad.
sites.description: The dedicated industrial manufacturing capital of the Indus world. Located 130 km south of Mohenjo-daro, it was exclusively populated by artisans, beadmakers, metal-casters, and seal cutters.

sites.name: Ganweriwala
key_structures: Dual-mound topography identical to Harappa and Mohenjo-daro
High western citadel mound and expansive eastern residential city
Located equidistant between Harappa and Mohenjo-daro on the dry Hakra bed
key_artifacts: Terracotta tablet depicting a cross-legged yogic figure and a kneeling worshipper
Steatite unicorn seal fragments
Pottery vessels with Indus graffiti signs
Terracotta bangles and copper implements
sites.foreign_connection: Crucial central hub on the Hakra river lifeline connecting the northern plains to the southern delta.
sites.description: A massive unexcavated metropolis sitting squarely in the center of the Hakra river system in the Cholistan desert, forming an equilateral triangle of power with Harappa and Mohenjo-daro.

sites.name: Alamgirpur
key_structures: Settlement on the bank of the Hindon River (tributary of Yamuna)
Mud-brick residential structures and refuse pits
Potters' kilns and storage silos
key_artifacts: Impression of woven cloth / textile on a trough
Ceramic platters, goblets, and perforated jars
Terracotta beads, animal figurines, and copper pins
Late Harappan painted pottery showing transition to Ochre Coloured Pottery (OCP)
sites.foreign_connection: Represented the extreme eastern frontier of the Indus Civilization, only 45 km from modern Delhi in the Ganga-Yamuna Doab.
sites.description: Marks the eastern boundary of the Harappan world, proving that Indus urban trade and material culture reached deep into the fertile plains of the upper Yamuna valley.

sites.name: Manda
key_structures: Fortified river outpost situated on the right bank of the Chenab River
Timber revetment and stone embankments
Himalayan foothill collection depot
key_artifacts: Copper spiral-headed pin (linking with Central Asian and Iranian cultures)
Indus script potsherds and inscribed seal fragments
Bone arrowheads and terracotta cakes
Harappan red ware jars and dishes-on-stand
sites.foreign_connection: Harvested Himalayan deodar cedar and pinewood, floated down the Chenab and Indus rivers for ship construction and roofing in Mohenjo-daro and Harappa.
sites.description: The northernmost bastion of the Indus Civilisation within modern India, positioned on the Chenab river in the foothills of the Pir Panjal range to secure Himalayan timber and minerals.

sites.name: Daimabad
sites.discovered_by: B.P. Bopardikar (1958); M.N. Deshpande and S.A. Sali
key_structures: Mud-brick multi-room houses on the left bank of the Pravara River
Craft quarter with copper smelters and crucibles
Granaries with carbonized wheat, barley, and lentils
key_artifacts: The Famous Daimabad Bronzes: A 45cm long solid bronze chariot driven by a man and pulled by two humped oxen
Heavy solid bronze elephant (29kg) on a platform with wheels
Solid bronze rhinoceros and water buffalo
Potsherds bearing incised Indus script signs
Steatite button seals
sites.foreign_connection: Linked the Deccan peninsula and Godavari valley to the Harappan trade orbit, accessing Deccan gold, semi-precious stones, and copper ores.
sites.description: The southernmost outpost of the Harappan civilization, located in Maharashtra. Astonished archaeologists with the discovery of four massive, solid-cast bronze sculptures weighing over 60 kg in total.

sites.name: Sutkagan Dor
sites.discovered_by: Major E. Mockler (1875); Sir Aurel Stein (1928); George Dales (1960)
key_structures: Massive stone fortification wall (over 7.5m thick at base) built on a natural rock ridge
Citadel with towers controlling the mouth of the Dasht River
Quayside landing steps for ocean vessels (now silted inland 50 km from modern coast)
key_artifacts: Copper axes and bronze spears
Pottery vessels with painted Harappan motifs
Stone blades and standard cubical weights
Beads of shell, steatite, and carnelian
sites.foreign_connection: Guarded the entrance to the Persian Gulf; the key maritime resupply station for Harappan cargo vessels sailing between the Indus delta and the Mesopotamian ports of Ur and Kish.
sites.description: The westernmost outpost of the Indus civilization, situated near the modern Iran border on the Makran coast. It served as a heavily fortified naval fortress and trading station for Gulf commerce.

sites.name: Shortugai (Lapis Lazuli Colony)
key_structures: Full Harappan brick architecture and street planning on the Oxus (Amu Darya) river
Canal irrigation network tapping the Kokcha River
Lapidary workshops for working raw lapis lazuli and tin
key_artifacts: Inscribed Indus steatite seals with unicorn and rhinoceros motifs
Pure lapis lazuli raw nodules, debitage, and polished cylindrical beads
Clay models of bullock carts and terracotta cakes
Standard Harappan painted black-on-red pottery identical to Mohenjo-daro
sites.foreign_connection: Direct Harappan commercial colony in Central Asia, established 1,000 km north of the Indus to directly control the legendary Badakhshan lapis lazuli mines and Central Asian tin sources for bronze casting.
sites.description: An astonishing distant colony established by the Harappans on the banks of the Amu Darya (Oxus) in Afghanistan. It granted the Indus merchants a complete monopoly over the global Bronze Age trade in lapis lazuli.

sites.name: Bhirrana
sites.period: Hakra Ware to Mature Harappan (7500–1900 BCE)
key_structures: Subterranean circular pit dwellings in the earliest Hakra phase
Multi-room mud-brick houses with paved hearths in mature phase
Complex underground drainage with terracotta soakage jars
key_artifacts: Red pottery shard engraved with a female figure in the exact pose of Mohenjo-daro's Dancing Girl
Lapis lazuli, carnelian, agate, and turquoise beads
Crucibles and copper bangles
Early Hakra Ware pottery with carbon-14 dates pushing back origin of IVC to 8th millennium BCE
sites.foreign_connection: Demonstrates the continuous, indigenous evolution of Indus culture along the Saraswati river system over 5,000 continuous years.
sites.description: Yielded the earliest radiometric carbon-14 dates in the subcontinent (c. 7570–7180 BCE), proving the deep indigenous antiquity of the pre-Harappan Hakra culture.

sites.name: Sinauli
sites.period: Late Harappan to Copper Hoard (2100–1800 BCE)
key_structures: Royal necropolis with 126 anthropomorphic burials
Wooden royal coffins adorned with copper repoussé anthropomorphic figures
Underground burial chambers with pottery offerings
key_artifacts: Three full-sized solid-wheeled bronze-plated chariots / horse carts
Copper antennae swords with solid hilt and leaf-shaped daggers
Composite copper and bone war helmets (shirastrana)
Gold and carnelian necklaces and torch-like copper shields
Eight-inch copper combs and mirrors
sites.foreign_connection: Showcases a martial, warrior elite during the Late Harappan transition in the upper Yamuna valley, reshaping understanding of Bronze Age warfare in South Asia.
sites.description: A landmark excavation in Uttar Pradesh that uncovered the subcontinent's first Bronze Age warrior chariots, copper swords with antenna hilts, and elaborately decorated royal coffins.

sites.name: Ur (Royal Cemetery of Ur)
sites.period: Mesopotamian Early Dynastic III to Akkad (2600–2100 BCE)
sites.badge: Indus Artifacts in Sumerian Royal Tombs
key_structures: Ziggurat of Ur and Royal Tombs of Sumerian Kings and Queen Puabi
Cuneiform administrative archives of Sumerian temple merchants
Quays of the Euphrates River connecting to the Persian Gulf
key_artifacts: Multiple square steatite Indus stamp seals inscribed with Harappan unicorn and script characters found in Sumerian graves
Etched carnelian beads with distinctive Harappan chemical alkali-bleached white geometric patterns
Standard Harappan cubical chert weights discovered in merchant houses
Cuneiform tablets of Sargon of Akkad (c. 2334–2279 BCE) bragging that 'ships from Meluhha, Magan, and Dilmun tied up at the quay of Akkad'
Cuneiform inscriptions mentioning Shu-ilishu, a certified 'Meluhha translator' residing in Mesopotamia
sites.foreign_connection: The ultimate destination of Harappan maritime trade. Meluhhan merchants lived in their own designated enclave at Guabba near Lagash, trading ivory, carnelian, lapis, gold, and timber for silver and wool.
sites.description: Excavated by Leonard Woolley, the royal graves of Ur yielded indisputable proof of direct Indus trade: authentic Harappan seals, etched carnelian jewelry worn by Sumerian queens, and cuneiform texts recording trade with Meluhha.

sites.name: Kish
key_structures: Monumental Palace of Kish and Ziggurats of Inanna and Zababa
Commercial warehouses and administrative quarters
key_artifacts: Classic square Harappan steatite stamp seals featuring the humped Indian bull and Indus script
Long barrel-cylinder etched carnelian beads made with Indus micro-drill technology
Inscribed sherds of Harappan black-slipped storage jars
Mesopotamian stone cylinder seals carved with Harappan animals (elephants and rhinos)
sites.foreign_connection: Major northern Sumerian consumer of Harappan luxury goods, receiving goods via the Euphrates river network.
sites.description: One of the most powerful ancient Sumerian city-states. Archaeological excavations recovered numerous Harappan seals and imported Indian carnelian beads in both domestic and temple contexts.

sites.name: Tell Asmar (Ancient Eshnunna)
sites.period: Early Dynastic to Old Babylonian (2500–1800 BCE)
sites.discovered_by: Henri Frankfort (1930-36, Oriental Institute of Chicago)
sites.badge: Indus Cylinder Seal with Elephant & Rhino
key_structures: Palace of the Rulers and Temple of Abu
Scribe school archives and merchant storage rooms
key_artifacts: Celebrated cylinder seal carved with an Indian elephant, one-horned rhinoceros, and long-snouted gharial (crocodile)
Etched carnelian beads identical to beads from Mohenjo-daro and Lothal
Indus-style square stamp seals and painted Indus pottery sherds
Indus chert weights conforming precisely to the 13.7g standard
sites.foreign_connection: Served as a key inland trade clearinghouse in the Diyala valley, receiving Indus goods transshipped through the Persian Gulf and overland via the Iranian plateau.
sites.description: Henri Frankfort's excavations uncovered unmistakable Indian fauna depicted on Mesopotamian seals alongside authentic Harappan carnelian beads and weights, providing critical cross-dating benchmarks.

sites.name: Susa (Capital of Elam)
key_structures: Acropolis of Susa and royal administrative complexes
Workshops connecting Persian Gulf trade with the Iranian plateau
key_artifacts: Over two dozen Indus stamp seals bearing Harappan script and unicorn motifs
Etched carnelian beads, shell bangles from the Indian Ocean (Turbinella pyrum)
Indus cubical chert weights
Elamite cuneiform texts recording trade with Meluhha for exotic animals, ivory, and lapis
sites.foreign_connection: The premier trade hub of the Elamite kingdom, linking Harappan maritime traders from the Gulf with overland caravans crossing the Iranian plateau toward Central Asia.
sites.description: Susa has yielded one of the largest concentrations of Indus seals outside South Asia, establishing the city as an essential diplomatic and commercial bridge between Meluhha and Elam.

sites.name: Failaka Island (Dilmun)
key_structures: Dilmun palace, temple complexes, and stone quayside installations
Warehouse storehouses for long-distance maritime shipping
key_artifacts: Circular Persian Gulf seals carved with classic Harappan unicorn and Indus script characters
Indus carnelian beads and Harappan weights
Chlorite vessels decorated in the Gulf dot-and-circle style
Harappan pottery storage jars with thick waterproof slip
sites.foreign_connection: Dilmun (modern Bahrain and Failaka) was the legendary middleman described in Mesopotamian texts as 'the place where the sun rises', mediating trade between Indus Meluhha and Sumer.
sites.description: An island outpost in Kuwait Bay that served as the primary offshore entrepôt for Dilmun merchants trading directly with Harappan ships sailing out of Lothal and Sutkagan Dor.

sites.name: Ras al-Jinz (Magan)
sites.discovered_by: Joint Hadd Project (Serge Cleuziou and Maurizio Tosi, 1985-2000)
sites.badge: Harappan Inscribed Storage Jars in Arabia
key_structures: Mud-brick maritime trading settlement (Building RJ-2) right on the Arabian Sea
Workshops for working green chlorite and processing Arabian Sea turtle shell and dried fish
Boat repair yards with bitumen slabs bearing impressions of reed hulls
key_artifacts: Large Harappan black-slipped storage jar sherds bearing incised Indus script signs
Copper ingots sourced from Omani mountain mines (the source of copper for both Indus and Sumer)
Indus steatite seal impression with composite beast
Carnelian beads, ivory combs, and shell ladles manufactured in Gujarat
Slabs of marine bitumen used for caulking Harappan trade ships
sites.foreign_connection: Identified as the ancient land of 'Magan', famed in Sumerian texts for copper and diorite. Harappan sailors made regular landfall here crossing the Arabian Sea.
sites.description: The easternmost tip of the Arabian peninsula where French and Italian archaeologists uncovered unambiguous evidence of Harappan seafaring merchants: authentic Indus jars, seals, ivory, and bitumen caulking.
